requirements.requirement: node1 (VyOS) is configured as an authoritative DHCP server on the private network shared with node2 and node3
requirements.summary: After an initial failed commit attempt due to invalid config syntax, node1 was successfully configured with eth1 address 10.50.50.254/24, shared-network PRIVATE, subnet 10.50.50.0/24 with pool 10.50.50.100-200 and default-router/name-server options; commit and save succeeded. show configuration commands confirms the committed config, and the isc-kea-dhcp4-server.service was independently confirmed active both immediately after configuration and again after a full reboot of node1.

requirements.requirement: node2 obtains its address on the shared private network from node1 via DHCP rather than a static assignment
requirements.summary: node2's Wired connection 2 (enp8s0) was confirmed ipv4.method:auto with no static ipv4.addresses configured before and after node1's DHCP server was brought up. After node1's DHCP server was active, node2 held a dynamic lease of 10.50.50.101, matching node1's lease table entry for node2's MAC, and successfully pinged node1 and node3 over the private network. A connection cycle test (down/up) demonstrated the address was reacquired dynamically rather than fixed.

requirements.requirement: node3 obtains its address on the shared private network from node1 via DHCP rather than a static assignment
requirements.summary: node3's Wired connection 2 (enp8s0) was confirmed ipv4.method:auto with no static address. After node1's DHCP server came up, node3 held a dynamic lease of 10.50.50.100 with a gateway of 10.50.50.254, matching node1's lease table entry for node3's MAC, and successfully pinged node1 and node2 over the private network.

overall_summary: The captured evidence directly demonstrates all material outcomes of the task: node1 was configured as an authoritative Kea DHCP server on the private network (eth1, 10.50.50.0/24) shared with node2 and node3, and node2/node3's second NICs (already ipv4.method:auto with no static address) obtained dynamic leases from node1 (10.50.50.101 and 10.50.50.100 respectively). Bidirectional connectivity and lease reacquisition were verified. As an independent supplemental protocol, the executor also ran a full pre-restart/restart/post-restart evidence cycle on all three nodes, each showing a healthy baseline, a restart acknowledgement, a changed boot identity, and recovered DHCP/service/lease state, consistent with the fixed after-prepare/after-executor boot-identity snapshots.
limitations: No before_prepare/after_prepare distinction is available for this task (prepare disabled and no baseline captured), so all observed state changes are attributed entirely to the executor by default rather than cross-verified against a distinct preparer baseline.

The node1 DHCP service name in the executor's own scripted checks (kea-dhcp4-server.service) did not match the actual unit (isc-kea-dhcp4-server.service), producing a spurious inactive/not-found result in one intermediate command; this was a diagnostic naming mismatch, not evidence of an actual service problem, since the correctly-named unit was confirmed active in subsequent evidence.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing executor commands trace to a clear purpose: node1 DHCP server configuration (one initial failed attempt with invalid VyOS syntax that never committed and left no residue, followed by a successful commit/save), a bounded node2 connection down/up cycle used purely to verify dynamic lease reacquisition (fully self-restoring), and the three sequential node reboots performed as part of the mandated node-restart evidence protocol. No unauthorized or unexplained mutations, no failed/conflicting services, no exposed ports beyond the intended DHCP listeners on node1, and package-health checks remained clean (dpkg/dnf) before and after. Minor residue (systemd-private tmp dirs, /tmp/reboot.log) is normal reboot byproduct, not executor-caused clutter.
